utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Whiting, I believe you have something to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just very briefly. It's in respect of the Defence submission of yesterday regarding the revised estimate of time for the witnesses, which raises some concerns -- a number of concerns for the Prosecution which I think can be solved very simply, if the Defence just files a motion seeking permission from the Court to lead its witnesses 89(F) or 92 bis. I would note that the Defence has now proposed, and I understand that this is at the urging of the Court, and it's entirely, in many ways, entirely appropriate, but they've now proposed that 18 witnesses be introduced by 89(F) - maybe now it's Rule 92 ter which applies - and five witnesses by 92 bis. That's a total of 23 witnesses, which is nearly half the Defence case going in by this method. The concerns that the Prosecution have are that -- well, number 1, that we receive notice; in other words, that the Defence file a motion with all the statements of all of these 23 witnesses that it proposes should go in 89(F) and 92 bis, and that the Prosecution and the Court can then -- well, the Prosecution can then take a position on it and the Court can rule on it. This would address a number of concerns that we have. Number 1, we're going to obviously need some advance notice -- we're going to have to have these statements in hand ahead of time in order to be able to prepare to cross-examine the witnesses. And by "ahead of time," not just a day ahead of time, I mean a week at least. Secondly, and this is the most important thing, we think that there may be some issues in the statements that should be led viva voce. The new rule 92 ter, which is essentially an expression of Rule 89(F) - it's kind of, you might say, a codification of Rule 89(F) - does allow for, in the discretion of the Court, for evidence about acts and conduct of the accused to be led via Rule 89(F). However, we would anticipate, and I can't be certain without seeing the statements themselves, that we may very well take the position, from the Prosecution side, that any critical -- any evidence about critical acts on conduct of the accused or evidence that goes to the central issues in this case should be led viva voce. It would be very odd, in our view, after having many witnesses who have testified for long periods of times without even mentioning Mr. Martic's name on direct examination one time, it would be very odd to then have critical evidence about the acts and conduct of the accused or about events that are central to this case go in on paper, which is essentially -- in a way, it's equivalent to the Defence just leading the witness through the examination-in-chief, because it's obviously -- on paper, the witness just says, Yes, I agree with that, and there is no real testimony. So we would anticipate making that distinction and identifying parts of the testimony that are critical that should be led viva voce. All of this to say that, in order to do that, in order to see if 89(F) is appropriate or how it is appropriate or 92 bis is appropriate there has got to be a motion with all of these 23 witnesses addressed and all of their statements provided to the Prosecution and the Court, and it has to be done in a timely fashion. Our last concern is the time that has been allotted by the Defence for cross-examination of these witnesses is obviously inadequate. For the 18 89(F) statements, we've been allotted an average of less than three hours per witness, according to the Defence schedule. Now, sometimes that may be appropriate with a narrow witness, a focused witness. But obviously if the statement that it goes in 89(F) covers a whole host of issues and a broad range of issues, we're going to need more than three hours to cross-examine the witness. And so that's another concern. But, of course, that can only be determined once we have the statements. So all of this to say that we would ask the Court to set a date with the Defence by which they will file a motion to address all of these 23 witnesses, so it can be done in an orderly way, the Rules can be applied appropriately, and we can come to a fair determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. The Chamber was planning to raise some of the issues that you have raised with the Defence. However, the underlying result of what I hear you saying seems to be to say, no, no, no, don't go 89(F) and don't go 92 bis because now we're going to want to cross-examine -- because we are going to want these people to testify viva voce on critical issues, when we have been trying to get the Defence to come under 92 bis. Obviously, I anticipate, and I think the Bench also anticipates, that some of those witnesses will come in for cross-examination. We do have a decision that we have passed in the past to say that witnesses coming through 92 bis must just come in and go straight into cross-examination without being fed or led, because of the confusion that was caused by the introductory leading, and then the cross-examiner wanting to go all over it, saying that this was mentioned in the introduction. So the hours that are allocated to 92 bis was simply entirely for cross-examination and some re-examination, if any, and questions from the Bench. But certainly no leading time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That is certainly my understanding, and that's the same for Rule 89(F). With respect to Rule 89(F), the witness is required to come in for cross-examination by the terms of the Rule. Just to be clear, Your Honour, I'm not discouraging, in any way, use of Rule 89(F) or 92 bis. I think it is appropriate. And it may -- what I am anticipating is that the most of the evidence, you know 90 per cent of the evidence, the background, the general things can come in 89(F) or 92 bis, but that the witness be led on critical issues, on the narrow part -- if there are any, in the witness's testimony. So there could be a combination of part of his evidence coming in 92 bis or 89(F) and part being led viva voce in court, which has been done in many cases before. But I am certainly not discouraging. I concur with the use of 89(F) and 92 bis, as long as it is done appropriately and according to the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But given the new 92 ter, the witness can come entirely on paper and just be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct. The Rule allows for even acts and conduct of the accused to come in on paper. However, we would anticipate urging a distinction between -- I mean, there are different kinds of acts and conduct of the accused. There can be acts and conduct of the accused which are cumulative or which are not that important or which are really agreed on. For example, the positions of the accused, if the witness is going to testify on that, they can come in on paper. But if they are critical issues, I think our view will probably be that those critical issues should be led live; otherwise, it is just leading the witness through the critical issues, which we've objected to up to now and it seems odd to go a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, does it still seem odd after the new 92 ter?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'm not saying it can't be done under the Rules. I agree it can be done, but the Rules simply say, it may -- it allows -- it's in the discretion of the Court that acts and conduct of the accused can be led -- put through paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But all I'm saying if the Court then so decides, the new 92 ter would be the reason for the odd appearance but also the explanation why it is odd.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But it is true the Rules allow for that. It just -- the fact is that evidence -- the reason we're not allowed on direct examination to lead a witness is because that goes to the weight of the evidence. That draws some questions about whether the evidence is really coming from the witness. Now, if that's about matters which are not critical to the case, it's fine. It doesn't really matter. There is no dispute about it. But with respect to disputed matters, we think those should be led live, viva voce, even given the new Rule 92 ter which allows the Court discretion about whether acts and conduct of the accused or what types of act and conduct of the accused should be led on paper or should be led viva voce. I'm not sure I'm making myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are coming loud and clear. Actually not only clear but also loud. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I'm not suggesting your voice is loud. I'm using the expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I see. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, Your Honour, with the decision of the Trial Chamber we were placed in a position where we had to act as told. Now the Prosecutor is expressing his concern over the fact that we are acting in accordance with the decision of the Trial Chamber, applying 92 bis and 89(F), without which we couldn't possibly comply. I think the Prosecutor should wait to see our submission and proposal and then see whether there is reason for concern, in the first place. However, I have a concern also, I mean we on the Defence team have a concern; namely, we are hearing live witnesses, we have complied with the obligation imposed on us by the Trial Chamber in their decision, and now we are in a position where we can't lead witnesses live at all, except in redirect. The main principle for us in every proceedings, including this one, is the principle of directness, live testimony. And this principle is in question if, in relation to half of the witnesses, only the Prosecutor can cross-examine and we can only do redirect. However, we suggest that time will show how we are going to cope with our obligation while applying 92 bis and 89(F).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, thank you so much. Regarding your first point, what you call the Prosecutor's concern, now, do understand that the Prosecutor needs to prepare his cross-examination of those witnesses, and I think his major concern so far as you are concerned is the expeditious delivery by the Defence of the motion and the attendant 92 bis and 89(F) summaries, so that they are able to do the cross-examination -- is it a summary or a full statement? Full statement, actually. So that they are able to prepare for their cross-examination. To that extent, I think you can disabuse your mind of any other concerns that the Prosecutor might have expressed, other than that one. I think that one is -- for your purposes, that's the main important concern. The other concerns, I think, are really addressed to the Chamber, and the Chamber will use its discretion as to which witness comes live and which witness comes viva voce on which issues. The Chamber will look at that. Your second concern, that the principle as you know it in every proceedings is that people testify live, indeed, I can't agree more with you, Mr. Milovancevic. That's the principle as I know it myself. Unless you are dealing with what, in my judicial culture, is called motion proceedings where you just do things on paper. Usually it's this way where no disputes of fact are anticipated. And if they do arise, then people come and testify. However, having said that, we both find ourselves in this international milieu, which has nothing to do -- which is different from our national jurisdictions, and we have got to adapt. Here we are now called upon to use 92 bis, to use 89(F), now there is the new 92 ter. We've got to use them. To the best of our abilities, we will make sure that -- and I think the concern you are expressing is the same concern that is expressed by Mr. Whiting. Where the witness comes to speak on very critical issues that go to the acts and conduct of the accused which are not necessarily cumulative or agreed or what have you, the Chamber may exercise their discretion, if so requested, to allow the witness to testify viva voce so that the Defence can lead him the best way they want to lead him and, of course, the witness's memory can be observed under in the witness box. I hope that answers your concerns and, to some extent, the Prosecution's.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I just wonder if we could set a date by which the Defence files its motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I was going to ask. Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting, for reminding me. Mr. Milovancevic, are you able to offer a date, without the Chamber imposing a time line on you? But also you remember that this needs to be done as soon as possible, because the Prosecution needs to prepare. Are you able to give a date by when you can do this? The most important thing is that the statements must be there for them to prepare.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. I would appreciate it if you would let me do that today, by the end of the day, but after the first session at least, so that I can consult my colleagues during the break, because we wish to give you a realistic assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Is that all, Mr. Whiting? Thank you. May I just raise something also from the Bench. The Chamber would like to request a 40-minute break -- the Chamber would like to ask for a 40-minute break at the end of this session. I don't see how we can recoup those minutes. We could break for 20 minutes in the next session, but the technicians need a full 30 minutes for the delayed relay. So it will just be ten minutes lost. Thank you very much. I'm sorry for eating into so much of your time, Mr. Perovic. May the witness come, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dragisic. May I take this opportunity just to remind you that yesterday, when you started testifying, you made the declaration to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. You are still bound by that declaration. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Dragisic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, if you recall, we dealt with the period between 1986 and 1990 when you were Chief of Staff of the Territorial Defence of Knin. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall us discussing it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: As regards the relationship between the staff of the Territorial Defence of Knin with the staff of the TO of the union of municipalities of Split, what is typically characteristic of this period, 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990 we had a perfectly normal relationship. Like before, they were our superior staff, and consistent with that we had a work plan for 1990, which we implemented by regularly sending reports and receiving orders from the Community of Municipalities of Split staff. Once a week, or sometimes more often, I travelled to Split to report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And that lasted until which moment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until January 1991, which was the last time I went to Split. But we still had regular communications by telephone until the end of March, 1991, and on several occasions commanding officers from the Community of Municipalities staff came to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that the commander of the union of municipalities staff was Ante Marinov. Do you remember what happened to him in 1990? He was Colonel Ante Marinov.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was still in that position, but in 1990, since he too received orders from the same superiors as I, he was replaced. But I don't know by whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was the main reason for his replacement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main reason was that Ante Marinov executed the orders of the General Staff, and he was committed to obeying the law on All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday that he was a Croat by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when the first multi-party elections took place in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, it was in the spring of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: After the multi-party elections, did there occur any changes in the composition of the General Staff or maybe the Territorial Defence of Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All the staff and all the commanding officers continued in their earlier positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: While we are at the multi-party elections in Croatia, the first ones, tell me, what do you remember most vividly about this electoral campaign preceding the elections?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the eve of the elections, they started glorifying the independent state of Croatia, the one from 1941 to 1945. In the press and on television, you could hear threats addressed to Serbs, namely threats that 1941 would happen again, more precisely that a genocide would be committed again against Serbs, a massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did certain state symbols change or were there any proposals to change them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just after the multi-party elections were over, when the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union, won in Croatia, the symbols changed. The five-pointed star was rejected and the Croatian symbol of the chequer-board was introduced and the Croatian coat of arms was introduced. All of those who wore uniforms received new black uniforms, not unlike those worn by Ustasha staff in 1941 to 1945.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What stance did the TO staff take vis-a-vis those new symbols?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We in the staff and the entire Serb population was against these changes because, in their minds, they were associated with the independent state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: While we are talking about the elections and the parties that took part, do you know if Milan Martic was a member of one of those parties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for a fact that he was not a member of any party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Was he a member of the Serb Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Relative to the change of symbols, state symbols, and iconography, did Mr. Martic have any problems in his work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did because he, like most of the policemen working in Knin, did not wish to take off the five-pointed star and receive the new symbol of the chequer-board, nor did they want to change the colour of the uniform into black.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did they take any steps? Did they do anything about it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wrote an open letter to the Federal Secretary for Internal Affairs in Belgrade, Mr. Petar Gracanin, and that letter was published in the daily Politika.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said "they." Who are "they"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Policemen from Knin. Over 50 of them signed that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And what became of them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their superior, the secretary of the SUP of the Sibenik, suspended four policemen from Knin that he designated as leaders: Milan Martic, Mr. Zelenbaba, Mr. Amanovic, and Mr. Cenic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: We have come to July 1990. As I say, that brings us to July 1990. Does the date 17 August 1990 ring any bells in your mind? Just a second. Speaking of that date, I want you to tell us only what you personally saw with your own eyes and what you remember.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, around the 25th of July, there was an Assembly in Srb which decided that the Serb people in Croatia would demand cultural autonomy. The referendum was scheduled for the 17th of -- for the 19th of August, 1990. On the 17th of August, that is two days before the referendum, Croatian authorities from Zagreb decided to stop the referendum from taking place and to stop it by force, and to do so by sending armed special units to take control of important features in Knin and stop the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you attend any meetings related to that in the Municipal Assembly of Knin? And what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 11.00 that day, I was invited by Mr. Milan Babic, through his secretary, to come to the Municipal Assembly building and meet with Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 11.00 of which day? And is this 11.00 in the morning or at night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the morning, on the 17th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So it was at 11.00 in the morning on the 17th of August, 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And what was the meeting about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chairman, Milan Babic, acquainted me very briefly with the situation and asked me to mobilize the Territorial Defence of Knin municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was your reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I replied to him that it was impossible to do, because he was not empowered to conduct a Territorial Defence mobilisation under the law, but the Territorial Defence staff of the Community of Municipalities, so Split, was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he ask you anything else at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He asked me whether I could take out weapons from the depots, of course referring to the weapons of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was your reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that that was impossible, too, because, according to the orders of the Presidency of the SFRY, the armaments were in the JNA depot at Krka.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this possibility -- you rejected this possibility offered to you by Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because he didn't have the powers, the competence to issue such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: At that time, so we are in August 1990, as I can see from your CV, you became the commander of the staff of the Territorial Defence of Knin. Who appointed you to that post?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Municipal Assembly of Knin, with approval from the staff of the Community of Municipalities of Split. The Community of Municipalities namely approved, endorsed my appointment, and the actual appointment was made by the Municipal Assembly of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Having become commander of the TO staff of Knin municipality, did you then talk, in connection with that, with Dr. Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What did he propose to you? What did he advocate in that talk with you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He proposed to me and demanded from me that we worked on the creation of a Serb army, an army that would not be commanded from Split or Zagreb or by the JNA, namely an army that he would be commander of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And what was your reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I refused. I didn't accept. I comported myself in accordance with the laws in force, the SFRY laws in force, and the valid laws of the Socialist Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So let us just accentuate this. This is a period in which the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia still existed, as did the JNA as its regular armed force; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, on that day, on the 17th of August, 1990, do you know what was happening in Knin in the afternoon, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that there was -- a story was bandied about that, from Zagreb, Split and other quarters, Croatian special units had set out, as well as helicopters from Zagreb, in the direction of Knin. And the people were very upset and frightened. They asked for arms. And they turned out in force in the streets, especially around the police station in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was happening right there in front, outside or inside the police station, the public security station at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, because I was summoned to the command of the 9th Corps, the JNA command in Knin, before a commission consisting of a general and two colonels. They asked me to give them a detailed report as to where the Territorial Defence weapons were, and they wanted to check whether anything had been taken out of the JNA depots.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know anything more specific about what was going on outside the public security station in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the date that we referred to, do you know whether the barricades were put up on that date? And how were they and why were they erected?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That evening barricades were put up primarily by -- in this way. Every year we, the Territorial Defence, the civil defence, would --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Dragisic. Tell me very briefly who initiated, who actually proposed the setting up of the barricades, and in what way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can the witness continue the first sentence? "Every year," he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. In the territories of all the municipalities, including the territory of Knin municipalities, exercises would be carried out. It was an action which was called "Nothing May Surprise Us," or "We Cannot Be Taken By Surprise," in which the entire population participated. And that was an exercise, combat actually, against saboteurs and the protection, security, of facilities, so that all the citizens knew what facilities were to be secured, where the barriers on the road were to be -- obstacles on the road were to be placed, and where saboteurs, if any, were to be followed. According to that scenario -- it was according to that scenario, more or less, that the blockade of the roads leading to Knin was actually carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Who actually was the initiator of the setting up of barricades; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that. Those were primarily the Serbian Democratic Party, which had won the elections in Knin municipality, in the local communes, and their activists were the ones who organised the erection of the barricades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we get some clarity here, Mr. Perovic. Witness, you said: "Every year the territories of all municipalities, including the territory of Knin, would have these exercises." Now, who would initiate these exercises every year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Earlier they would be initiated by the Socialist Alliance, which was the widest party that existed. It was in charge of that and it also participated. The army, to a lesser extent and the Territorial Defence and the civil defence and work organisations, enterprises, also participated in such exercises. So we can say the committee and the Socialist Alliance, as it was called at the time, namely the then existing socio-political organisations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So in this year, did the army and the Territorial Defence and the civil defence also participate in the initiation of this, like every year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This year, after the multi-party elections, there were no more exercises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. But when you were asked about the barricades, you told us about what happens every year, linking the two. So there was an exercise in the form of barricades. Now I'm asking you: Did the army and the TO and the civil defence also participate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the erection of barricades participated only the citizens. The people organised by the Serbian Democratic Party, the army, the Territorial Defence and the civil defence did not participate, and that is in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why did they not participate? This is their annual activity. Why don't they participate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no longer any such preparations. It was not anymore an exercise, nor was there anyone asking for that exercise to be carried out, because when exercises were undertaken, they would be organised from Zagreb and the directions would come from Zagreb. And that was no longer the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So, if I understood you correctly, the staff of the Territorial Defence in Knin had nothing whatsoever to do with the barricades. I'm referring to the initiative for and the organisation of the barricades.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Dragisic, on that day, the 17th of August, 1990, did Milan Babic declare a state of war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, and he did it via Radio Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And you, as the Territorial Defence Staff, reacted to that how, to that proclamation of his?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I immediately informed the staff of the Community of Municipalities and the command of the 9th Corps of the JNA, and the staff undertook no steps in that connection at all. Only from the Community of Municipalities staff, they asked us to organise constant round-the-clock duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did you put on uniforms at the invitation of Milan Babic, i.e., mobilize?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that was not according to the law, and he was not empowered to issue such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: All right. Just one moment. Were the people who put up the barricades empowered to put up barricades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were people from the Serbian Democratic Party who organised that, and the people organised themselves because of a threatening danger that the armed special unit members in armoured personnel carriers, aboard helicopters and with weaponry, would occupy the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You gave a very long answer, but up to now you have not gone to the substance of my question. I asked you whether they had the power to put up the barricades. You have been mentioning the fact that Mr. Babic didn't have the power to do a number of things. Could you answer the question, please? Did they, by law, have the power to put up the barricades? Was it their duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, have you heard of a body called the Council of People's Resistance? What was this body and how did it come into being?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the multi-party elections in Knin, the Serbian Democratic Party won, and Milan Babic was elected the president of the Municipal Assembly. Up to that time there had existed a body called the Committee for All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection. The very designation "committee" was reminiscent of communism. Babic did not want and organ called a committee, but redubbed, renamed this committee, this organ, this body, into the Council of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, who decided on the membership of that body?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That decision was made by Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was the task of that body?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he would issue some communiques on Radio Knin which were principally of a political content.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Until when was this Council of National Resistance operational?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It issued its communiques until the establishment of the SAO Krajina on the 19th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Which is when the Council of National Resistance practically ceased to exist?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So you said it was on the 19th of December, 1990, that the SAO Krajina was proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: From that moment, what was the attitude towards the Territorial Defence Staff in Croatia, in Zagreb namely?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We - and I personally, as the commander - continued to maintain correct relations, and my superior command was the Community of Municipalities staff. And, as I already said, in January I travelled to Split. I submitted a report there. And nothing changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Then, at that time, did Dr. Babic give you any proposals related to the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What did he insist on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He insisted on the establishment of a Serb army and the setting up of detachments and regiments, Chetnik regiments and detachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was your position vis-a-vis that proposal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position and the position of my staff was that we wouldn't, couldn't accept that, because there existed the JNA, i.e., the armed forces of the SFRY, and we were a part of those forces and we did not want to be outside that particular framework.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Let me move away from this topic a bit and ask you this: Have you ever heard of Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When did that man appear in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in the second half of April, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I apologise for the interruption. This is not the first time that we've gone beyond the 65 ter summary, but there's -- as far as I can see, there is just nothing that -- no mention of Captain Dragan or anything that would even arguably bring this within the purview of the summary. So I would object to this evidence being led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I acknowledge the objection and I accept it. It's just that I was misinformed by my associates regarding the contents of the summary. The objection is completely justified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. Are you then going to withdraw the question, Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, we are now in April 1991. At that time, did there occur a deterioration of the security situation; and if it did, why?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did, because on Easter day, on the 31st of March, special units of Croatia attacked the special units of Krajina at Plitvice, resulting in the first casualties and the capture of 13 or maybe 16 members of the Krajina police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When did the tensions between the sides grow particularly high? Due to which incident?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After these men were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You mean that incident at Plitvice that you described? I'm asking you about another incident that maybe complicated the situation even further.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May, in Borovo Selo, there was a skirmish between Croatian police and the Krajina police in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What about the area immediately around you? Did something happen that disturbed the residents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On that 2nd of May, Vaso Pecar was killed, a person from Polaca, he was killed by the residents of Kijevo. That really caused great unrest, both in Polaca itself and the broader area of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When was the first government of SAO Krajina established? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 29th of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Who became head of that government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first head of government and Minister of Defence became Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Then, as the newly appointed Minister of Defence, what did he advocate in his contacts with you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He kept insisting on the establishment of the Serbian Army of Krajina, but once the government of Krajina was established, along with the Assembly of Krajina, he had the authority to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was your opinion on the matter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I continued to impose it because in the framework of the SFRY --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But what was the position of Milan Martic on this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said you were against those initiatives of Mr. Babic. What about Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Mr. Martic was also in favour of cooperating with the JNA. He was against the rejection of the five-pointed star and against the changes of emblems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, so as not to break your train, I have elected to ask the question at the end of the day, if necessary. Please proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: We are now in the summer of 1991. What is typical of this period, June, July, and later in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The month of June saw a deterioration of general relations. Slovenia and Croatia, sometime around the 25th of June, unilaterally and unlawfully proclaimed their independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the territory of Croatia? What happened there in the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That summer, the Croatian Democratic Union, i.e., the Croatian authorities with their paramilitary army that they named Home Guard Corps, including policemen without proper training, imposed blockades on JNA barracks throughout Croatia, cutting off their electricity, water supply, and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was the response of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA General Staff adopted the decision to partially mobilise JNA units in afflicted areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: How was that order on partial mobilisation reflected on the defence of Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was ordered that younger men, that is conscripts below the age of 55, would have their military files turned over to the JNA with a view to including them in reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So conscripts younger than 55 were mobilised into the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was the position of Milan Babic regarding this order to mobilise?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think he accepted it because there was nothing he could do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So, for all practical purposes, who remained in the TO units, in the units of the Territorial Defence, after this mobilisation into the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only unfit people, people not fit for combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So how were the Territorial Defence units organised after June 1991 and after that decision to mobilise?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, the territorial principle prevailed. Units were organised in local communes, but since most men, including commanding officers, were mobilised into the JNA, the resulting TO units did not have good commanding staff, and those who were in command were not qualified to train and to lead units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Were they fit for combat, these units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In August 1991, in your area, did the army undertake any operations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The action to lift the blockade off Kijevo, Kijevo being a local commune behind which there were more villages belonging to the municipality of Knin, populated by Serbs, whereas Kijevo was a predominantly Croat place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What I want to know, really: Were Territorial Defence units involved in any way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe there was one platoon from Lapac or somewhere, but the Territorial Defence did not take part from in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What happened to you personally in September 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since those units, less than ready as they were, had to hold positions on the periphery, on the outskirts of the municipality, I inspected those units and showed them how to create shelters, how to make cover, because a mortar can wound or kill a fighter by wounding him even in the back, if he is not covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So what happened then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I ended up wounded in the area of Velika Glava.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An 82-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Where did the projectile come from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the positions of Croatian paramilitary forces, from the territory of Sibenik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: After you were wounded, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was hospitalized in the Military Medical Academy in Belgrade for about three months, which was followed by rehabilitation until May next year.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The VMA, the Military Medical Academy is in Belgrade, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When did you go back to Knin, and to what position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around the new year. And starting with 1st June 1992, I was on the teaching staff in the military training centre in Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What about the training centre in Golubic, who were the trainees and what were they trained for?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The trainees were citizens of Krajina and citizens of Croatia, up to 27 years, who had no criminal record, and they were trained to become beat policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So policemen. So those young men who completed this course in Golubic could become beat policemen, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And if they wanted to advance in that profession, what did they have to do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, with the assistance of senior policemen in police stations, they had to prepare themselves to apply for enrollment in the higher school of internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask this once again: After completing the course in Golubic, they could only become policemen.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after a trial period of one month. Each one of them had a mentor who trained him after completing the course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The young men who were trained during that course, were they ever used in combat?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, I do not have any further questions to ask you in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. Mr. Black, do you think you can start now, or do you think we can come back later?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm happy with taking a break now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's take a break now. We will come back at five to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, my name is Mr. Black. I'm a member of the Prosecution team, and I am going to be asking you questions for a while now. First of all, you said that you are married; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If you don't mind me asking, what is your wife's name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedjelka.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Does she have any family relationship with the accused, Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she's his sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you are, in fact, the accused's brother-in-law; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified that whereever possible TO weapons were stored in JNA weapons depots in order that the weapons be secured. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What time frame were you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the end of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what about -- when were you saying that that started? When were the TO weapons first held in a JNA weapons' depots, according to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were there since the very inception of the Territorial Defence, so I suppose sometime from 1970 onwards. And the depot was in the JNA depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Isn't it actually the case that it was only in May of 1990 that the JNA took control of TO weapons and put them in JNA depots? That only happened in May of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not correct. Wherever it was possible, with a view to security measures, the TO weapons were in JNA depots. Some municipalities, which were far away from garrisons, had a part of the -- held themselves a part of the weaponry. But that was not the case with Knin municipality, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at a document. It's Exhibit 409 in evidence in this case, and it will come up on the screen in front of you in just a moment, sir. Sir, look with me at this document. You'll see that this is a document from the Main Staff of the SFRY. It's dated the 14th of May, 1990. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But I should like to tell you how this was solved in Knin municipality. Actually I told you how this question was dealt with in Knin municipality, and that is definitely correct, namely Knin municipality never had another depot because of the practical considerations, namely it should have had security guards and they should be paid, and if it was with the JNA, that was unnecessary. I'm familiar with this order but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So you're familiar with this order. So you're saying that in Knin, the TO weapons were in the JNA weapons depot even before this order. But you accept, don't you, that elsewhere in Croatia, TO weapons would have been stored separately from the JNA weapons.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened in very few municipalities. For instance, Obravac, in Benkovac -- kept their weapons in the Benkovac garrison; Gracac in the Sveti Rok garrison; Sinj in the Sinj garrison; and Split in the Split garrison. Only municipalities which were quite far away from the garrisons kept a part of the weapons separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The places that you've mentioned are mostly in Krajina or there in Dalmatia. What about the rest of Croatia? The other places in Croatia, the TO weapons may have been stored separately or would have been stored separately from the JNA weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Wherever it was possible, the weapons were kept in JNA garrisons. So that, for instance, the TO of Knin --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let's look at this, at paragraph 1 of this order. You can follow along with me. It says -- it talks about the military district, et cetera, and it says: "They shall organise the takeover, storage and safekeeping of the complete stock of the TO weapons and ammunition in the JNA supply dumps and depots." That's what it says; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a question before you go on. It doesn't make any sense to issue an order like this if the TO weapons are already in the JNA depots, does it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very small quantity. For instance, if the Territorial Defence Staff has 2.000 barrels, pieces of barrels, which was retained -- 20 or 30 barrels would be retained for the anti-sabotage unit, and that would be stored in the TO depot, because they could be quickly taken out and issued from the depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If what you say is true, why would the SFRY General Staff issue an order like this, if the effect of it really only touched on a very, very small percentage of TO weapons? It doesn't make any sense, does it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall answer that in this way: At that time, when this order was passed, abusing the right to retain a small number of pieces of weaponry, for instance, two or three crates, boxes, certain staffs, whose commanders had been replaced and where HDZ had appointed the commanders, actually retained more weaponry, which they had removed from the JNA depots. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you're saying that some TOs, which already in May 1990 were controlled by the HDZ, you say that those were the depots -- or those were the TO staffs that were keeping their weapons separate from the JNA depots; right? That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I'm saying is that they had to keep their weapons in the JNA depots, but they wrote orders to the effect that they were conducting exercises and they drew from these supplies, from the depot, weapons which they wouldn't return.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you say this happened in TOs which were controlled by the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you aware that Borislav Jovic, who was at that time was the chairman of the SFRY Presidency, he's described this order as the disarming of the TOs, and said that it happened over the objection in Croatia of Slovenia? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It wouldn't make any sense for him to view this order as disarming the TOs if only a small percentage of TO weapons were outside of JNA depots, even before the order; right? That wouldn't make any sense.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this subject matter well, and I assert that the situation is definitely as I described it and it is very viable, by whatever means you have at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, the question was, it doesn't make sense, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I adhere to what I have said, and I know for a fact that it was so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question was: It doesn't make sense, does it? Does it make sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it doesn't make sense, but if you accept my explanation - and I adhere by it - that is the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So, according to you, this order that we see before us, that didn't have the effect of disarming the TOs; in fact, it had only a negligible effect because such a small percentage of TO weapons were held outside of JNA depots before May of 1990; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you say that if Borislav Jovic described it differently, then he was simply wrong, despite the position that he had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Borislav Jovic said, but I know what the situation was in all the 22 municipalities in Dalmatia, and I think that they all stored -- kept their weapons in JNA depots.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, why don't we just briefly look at what Borislav Jovic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And it is Exhibit 476, please. Thank you. In English, the page I'm looking for has 03022947 at the top, and in B/C/S it's 01157807. And in just a moment I hope I can tell you exactly which that is, because as we've seen before with this document, it's just excerpts there. THE USHER: 7807, the last four --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think it is 7807. It's the entry for the 17th of May, 1990. THE USHER: In English?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In B/C/S. In English it is 032022947, and it says "page 131" at the bottom. I apologise, I should have been more prepared with the exact page number. It's page 11 in the e-court number in B/C/S. That's the correct page in B/C/S. I'm not sure if you're able to find the English page okay. Okay, great, we're ready to go. Sorry for the delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, look there at the entry for the 17th of May, and this is actually from the published diary of Borislav Jovic. He says there: "17 May 1990. We take measures to ensure that weapons are taken from civilian Territorial Defence depots in Slovenia and Croatia and transferred to military depots. We will not permit Territorial Defence weapons to be misused in any conflicts or for forcible secession. Practically speaking, we have disarmed them." Now, what Mr. Jovic, the chairman of SFRY Presidency, says here, that they were disarming the TOs, that doesn't make any sense if the TO weapons were already in JNA depots, does it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it doesn't. But I claimed that all the weapons in all the 22 Dalmatia municipalities were in JNA depots. And if you ask me to comment on this, the Presidency of the SFRY is the supreme commander under the law and it was within their powers to issue an order of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you're saying that you know better than the chairman of the SFRY Presidency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: -- what the actual situation was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I would think that this issue has been covered enough, because the witness, didn't he say that there were certain abuses in the Croatian, majority Croatian areas of Croatia, and that -- and on the other side, you yourself said that this diary note of Mr. Jovic addressed the issue of secession of Slovenia and Croatia. So it wouldn't especially --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had understood the witness to suggest that only a very small percentage of TO weapons were held outside the JNA depots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No. He said, actually, on page 33, line 5, he told us, he informed us, about the so-called exercises when orders were issued to take out the weapons and then they were retained by, sort of, tricks, and that was quite plausible, I would even say. So I don't really understand insisting --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, I'm going to change topics now. When discussing the 1990 elections, you said that there were threats of genocide against the Serbs. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you name any person who threatened genocide against the Serbs, who used that word, "genocide," in the campaign for the 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you another question. That was really just the interpretation of Serb leaders and Serb media of what was happening throughout Croatia in the election campaign; right? That was the Serb interpretation of events. It wasn't any explicit threat, by anyone on the Croatian side, of genocide.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but in the town, downtown in the cafes, Ustasha songs would be sung. There would be graffiti on the walls that Serbs should hang on willows, and similar stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But no Croatian leaders used the word "genocide" or threatened a genocide against the Serbs in 1990, in that election campaign; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't utter such threats. But immediately upon their victory, they invited the Ustasha criminals, who had been indicted for war crimes in the Second World War, for instance, Ivo Rojnica and Sakic, and they immediately returned to Croatia to attend the HDZ congress in the Lisinski conference hall. So these were all Ustasha criminals, indictees, indicted for war crimes. At that time they came from the Argentine and other countries. They all came to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You answered my question when you said, "No, they didn't utter such threats." So unless I ask you for more information, you don't need to go on further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: In fact, that was the issue, these announcements before the election. I would like to refer to your statement which didn't expressly speak of official statements, but you said at page 11, line 22: "On the eve of the elections," you remember you said, "they started," they, whoever, "started glorifying the independent state of Croatia, the one from 1941 to 1945, in the press and on television." And then you spoke of threats. But I would like to ask you in this context, what do you mean by glorifications of the one or two times in the press and on television? What press and what television are you referring to? And who was that, then, in these media, official persons or journalists or party members, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For instance, Dr. Tudjman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: We are speaking of glorifying the independent state of Croatia, the one from 1941 to 1945, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On television, they would organise talk shows, inviting as guests people who would talk about what the borders of Croatia used to be, all the achievements of that period; that it was the 1.000-year aspiration, wish of the Croatian people. So these were people who would become deputies later, and they spoke in this way in the electoral campaign, and they also referred to the programme they would be implementing once they were elected, once they were in power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So this is what you mean by "glorification of the state from 1941 to 1945"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, in that same testimony that His Honour just asked you about, you continued, actually, and you said, and I will quote you: "You could hear threats addressed to Serbs, namely threats that 1941 would happen again, more precisely, that a genocide would be committed again against Serbs." My question is: You didn't actually hear that. No one threatened that a genocide would be committed again against the Serbs, did they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear that. For instance, after my arrival in Split, when I went to the community or municipality staff to submit my report, five or six lads --.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you talking about the --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So five or six young men were walking down the street singing songs. I cannot recall the exact songs, but in the songs they sang about the Ustashas. And on the walls, also, there were all sorts of slogans written threatening the Serbs, for instance, the one that I mentioned, hang up the Serbs on willow trees and the like. This also was the case in Zagreb and in other cities which I visited. And, of course, I cannot say -- talk about the other ones which I didn't visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, you didn't hear this from Croatian leaders; right? You're saying you could hear songs in different towns; people using graffiti, it sounds like. But this wasn't statements of Croatian leaders, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about the time before the elections -- I am talking about the time before the elections, and heading the Croatian government at that time were people from the Socialist Republic of Croatia who did not utter such statements. So that the Serbs living in towns voted en masse for the Socialist Party that had been in power until that point in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. We didn't hear these kinds -- no one from the HDZ, not Croatian government authorities but Croatian leaders in the HDZ in the election campaign, no one from the HDZ threatened to commit genocide against the Serbs, did they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, neither in 1941 did they utter such threats, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the election campaign in 1990, because you told us, at page 11 of the transcript, that threats were addressed to Serbs, precisely that a genocide would be committed again against Serbs. My question to you is: No HDZ leaders said that, did they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but the following happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But before you go on --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on the apartments of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, we're talking about statements. Threats, because that's what you talked about, right, no HDZ leader made such threats of committing genocide against the Serbs, did they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that that was the Croatian state, that the Croats would take over control in the state. They did not say that they would be killing people, but it was understood from what I'm saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. But there is a big difference, isn't there, between wanting independence for Croatia and committing genocide against the Serbs. Those are two totally different things, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they are not, because we simply did not dare -- I didn't dare go to Split, to Rijeka, to Zagreb any more, because the atmosphere was such and people -- and, of course, you know that the Serbs speak a bit differently. And we had problems going to such places. And I was afraid. Not only I. All of the Serbs who travelled to these places were very much afraid of what might happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Afraid of Croatian independence, not afraid because Croatian leaders were threatening a genocide against the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not afraid of independence. I was afraid that I might be killed, because already then such things started happening. People were going missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You see, just a moment ago you told us that what the Croatian leaders -- that they didn't say anything about killing people, but they talked about -- that it was going to be a Croatian state. What I don't understand is how talking about having a Croatian state led you to fear a genocide. It wasn't anything stated by the Croatian leaders. That was kind of your interpretation and the interpretation of the Serb leadership and media; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. At that time I was working at the Municipal Assembly of Knin. Until then, whenever we would come to work, we would drink coffee together, Serbs and Croats together, and we worked closely together. Then, all of a sudden, the Croat employees, our co-workers, stopped talking to us except when they had to officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me try to just wrap this topic up in one question, sir. When you told us at page 11 of the transcript that you could hear threats precisely that a genocide would be committed against the Serbs, that's not true; right? You were exaggerating or you were giving an interpretation. But you didn't hear threats of genocide against the Serbs, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly didn't exaggerate. It's the same thing as being able to feel cold or warmth, you know. Just like you feel you're cold or you're warm, I felt that I was in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You felt that you were in danger, but you do agree with me - and I think you said this but it's so confusing because you're kind of going back and forth - you do agree that although you felt this danger, it wasn't because leaders of the Croatian government or leaders of the HDZ were actually threatening genocide; right? This was just something that you felt, you and other Serbs, I think.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I give you another example?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, first answer my question, and then if it is necessary to give another example, you can.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not said explicitly. But I'm telling you, if suddenly you find writing on the wall that was clean the day before, "Kill the Serb," or you go to a football match and you see this murderous crowd, you cannot feel fine any more. You don't feel it is all right any more. It's not that a politician publicly uttered it, but at football matches, in everyday conversations, it was a distinct feeling that you had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry. So what would people at football matches say? Presumably they would be Croats. My microphone isn't ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went to see a football match between Hajduk and Zvezda, the last one that was held in Split. I went with my children. And when they started chanting "Look at them gypsies, kill them," I had to leave there, the stadium. I had to leave with my children. I feared for my own safety and the safety of my children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So who would be "gypsies"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's a derogatory term the Croats used for Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, I'm going to move you to a different topic now. I would like to focus your attention on the 17th of August, 1990. You testified about barricades being erected on that day, and I think I understood you to say that facilities were secured in Knin at the same time that the barricades were erected. Did I understand that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you did not, because in Knin there was no need to secure any facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Because earlier today, and it was at page 17 of the transcript, you talked about the exercises from before and you said that: "It dealt with protection and security of facilities so that all the citizens knew what facilities were to be secured, where the barriers were to be, obstacles on the road, et cetera." And then you said: "It was according to that scenario, more or less, that the blockade of the roads leading to Knin was actually carried out." So that is why I asked it. But in that context, were any facilities secured in Knin on the 17th of August, 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For my education, what is meant by "facilities"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, facilities are understood to be, for instance, hospitals, the building of the Municipal Assembly, the water reservoir, sources of water, a bridge across the river, similar things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, in response to a question from Her Honour Judge Nosworthy, you said that the barricades were not authorised; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, when panic spread among the Serb population in Knin because they were afraid that special units were coming, armed with weapons, tear gas and armoured vehicles, it was the initiative of the citizenry themselves to put up roadblocks to stop vehicles that might come from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, you explained before how this was organised and whose initiative it was. My question to you is: They were not authorised; right? The erection of the barricades was illegal, basically.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened on that 17th of August when roadblocks were put up through the SDS and Dr. Babic had proclaimed the state of war over the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. You have explained that. Let me go back to what you said before. Judge Nosworthy asked you a very specific question. She said: "Did they," referring to the people who erected the barricades, "did they, by law, have the power to put up the barricades? Was it their duty?" And you said: "No".

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So just to -- so I understand that right, that these were unauthorized barricades, they were not lawfully established barricades. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and they were erected unlawfully by people who were acting out of fear --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, let me just stop --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- driven by fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the motivations. I just asked you if they were lawfully established or not, and you responded to that right away. Did the police or the authorities in Knin take any action to remove these illegal barricades?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
