utterances.text: The next day the police authorities demanded that the barricades be removed. However, from the other side, Croat policemen from outside the municipality put up their check-points. And the men who worked in Sibenik and that general area would have to produce their IDs, were taken to the police station --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and were stopped from entering the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about barricades set up by Croats, wherever you say that happened. I'm asking you about the barricades that you talked about, the ones that you testified about, set up by Serbs, okay? Are you saying that the Serb police authorities demanded, on the 18th of August, that the barricades be removed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Who demanded that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who it was in the police force who demanded it, but the demand was made for barricades to be removed and for civilians to return their weapons. Dr. Raskovic demanded that the police enforce that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: On the 18th of August, Milan Martic was in charge of the barricades, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I had my own job to do. I was not a member of the council. Well, Milan Babic was the boss and he was in charge of everything, except the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This is your brother-in-law we're talking about, right, the one you say that you don't know what he was doing on the 18th of August, 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You mean the brother-in-law? I don't know what he was doing, because I had my own job to do, as I said. I had to make sure that my entire equipment and everything else was in place. I submitted my reports. And I did not meet with Martic on that day or the next few days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I ask: Was the accused, Milan Martic, already at that time your brother-in-law? May I ask in this context, when did you marry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1974, but as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I get the picture. Thank you. That's fine. You may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, surely you learned then after that, that in the coming days and the days after the 17th of August, 1990, that Milan Martic was in charge of the barricades; right? Whether you knew that on the 18th or not, you learned that later; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the SDS was in charge of the barricades, not Milan Martic. It was not the police who had control over the barricades. It was local communes, together with the SDS, that had control, because there was not enough police to man them. Every local commune controlled the barricades in their own territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You do agree with me, though, that police participated in the manning of the barricades; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there was a policeman Knezevic who was in charge of the barricade near Vrlika, but I don't know about the other barricades. You will agree with me that I had my hands full with the Territorial Defence and had nothing to do with the barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You said that in your view, on the 17th of August when there were these rumours of Croatian APCs and helicopters coming to Knin, that that was intended to prevent the referendum; right? That's what you had told us earlier.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No helicopters or APCs ever arrived in Knin, did they, on the 17th of August, 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. But the next day we heard news that JNA aircraft had turned back aeroplanes that were already flying towards Knin, JNA aircraft made them turn back towards Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But, in fact, that didn't happen either. Those aircraft, if there were aircraft, turned back for other reasons. They were never intercepted by JNA aircraft, were they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were intercepted and forced to turn back. It was in the newspapers, and we also received the same information from the 9th Corps of the JNA. We received information that planes had taken off from the military airport in Lucko and JNA aircraft made them turn back. It was reliable information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The other operation or operations on that day - and I'm thinking about Benkovac in particular, where the Croatian authorities actually did seize weapons from the reserve police forces - those operations were not about the referendum; they were about ensuring control of reserve police weapons so that they wouldn't be used by policemen who were actually hostile to the Croatian authorities; right? That was the real purpose of that operation in Benkovac and the failed operation in Obravac on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs were being disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's right. And it didn't have anything to do with the referendum; it was about ensuring control of the reserve police weapons in those towns, Benkovac and they tried in Obravac; right? That's what it was really about.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Police were being disarmed in places populated by Serbs. And you must know that there was a film shown on TV in which General Spegelj advises Croat --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- activists how to kill officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: We had other evidence about this film so I am going to interrupt you there. You know, you said Serbs were being disarmed, but they weren't disarming Serbs. What they were doing was taking control of police weapons that belonged to the Croatian MUP. Right? The Croatian MUP was taking control of its own weapons; that's what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs were also part of the Croatian MUP. However, their weapons were seized. Serbs in Benkovac and Knin also belonged to the Croatian MUP, but they no longer had the right to hold weapons; Zadar and Split seized it from them. And there was a request to approve the removal of weapons from reserve police, and that permission was granted. And about 500 weapons were removed from the Subicevac depot by MUP Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let's take this one step at a time. One, you agree with me that these weapons, these reserve police weapons were the property of the Croatian MUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the ownership of the police --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But the --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and it was distributed across all the public security stations. And depending on the number of reserve policemen in a particular station, they had an appropriate number of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It was in the ownership of the Croatian MUP, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was owned by the entire police force, but each police had their own weapons. And now --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, let me stop you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- wherever there was Serb population --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you say it was owned by the entire police force, that's the Croatian MUP; right? That's the police force we're talking about. Just please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but Serbs also belonged to the Croatian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, please answer my question. I'm not disputing who, whether it was Croats or Serbs that belonged to the Croatian MUP. I'm talking about weapons. They were the property of the Croatian MUP. Correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that there were --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. It's correct. That's all we need to do. Now I can move on to the second part of my question. Serb policemen were not disarmed. No one removed their right to carry arms, the right to hold weapons, as you said. It's simply that the reserve police weapons in Benkovac were seized by their owners, the Croatian MUP; right? That's what happened. Not disarming of Serb police.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it happened this way: In civilian uniforms, carrying rifles, they came by night and removed those weapons. Do you call that lawful disarming? It was more like a raid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I ask the questions here, not you, okay?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, what do you mean, "civilian uniforms"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The way I'm dressed now, or in jeans. People came on trucks, carrying rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not a uniform. Is that a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. In civilian clothes, because it was summertime and some were wearing jeans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And one more thing about the referendum and the barricades. The referendum was actually held as scheduled, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You've told us who you say initiated the barricades, the SDS. But, in fact, the coordination and the organisation of the barricades was done by the staff of the defence of Knin which was later renamed the Council for National Resistance; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably from the moment when I left that council at 11.00, I no longer took part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why "probably"? You should be able to tell us definitively whether, when you left at 11.00, you never took part. Why is it probable that you never took part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not take part. But to the question asked by the gentleman as to who was in charge of that, I suppose it was the Council for National Resistance, headed by Babic. And Lazar Macura was a member, and I don't know who the other members were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, this is supposed two sentences. There should be a full stop after the word "probably," I suppose. Okay, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you saying, sir, that after 11 in the morning on the 17th of August, 1990, you don't know who coordinated the barricades?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know, because I was summoned to come before a JNA commission at the corps command and that commission was trying to establish whether the weaponry was distributed to the Territorial Defence or not. And after that I reported to the staff of the Community of Municipalities and I stayed at the Municipal Assembly building. But I heard from my co-workers that there was a large crowd outside the police station, and I later found out that, at the mobilisation assembly point in the Golubici settlement, arms were being distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Those arms were being distributed by Milan Martic; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that and I cannot testify to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, you said you heard about it, and you also heard that Milan Martic was one of the people distributing the weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that the police was distributing weapons. I did not hear that Milan Martic specifically did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me focus back again on the Council for National Resistance. You told us about where you were on the day of the 17th of August, 1990, but after that day and going on into September, you were a member of the Council for National Resistance, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the working of the Council for National Resistance at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know only what I heard from Radio Knin. There were occasionally communiques from the Council for National Resistance. But I did not take part in its work and I know only what I heard on the radio. I think Milan Babic led that council.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, on the one hand, you say you don't know, and then now you say you think Milan Babic led the council. Do you know who led the council?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Babic led everything, not only the council. He was supreme commander. He was president of the municipality, president of the Assembly. He held all of the positions. Whatever was going on, he wanted to be in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, in what capacity was Milan Babic a supreme commander in August of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August 1990, he could not have been a commander. If you listened to me, I explained that the Territorial Defence was subordinated to the staff of the Community of Municipalities, and the other thing was subordinated to the supreme -- to the General Staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to the republican staff, sorry. So at that time he was only president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This seems to have been a matter for a clear expression that he was supreme commander, sort of ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So when you said that -- when you used the word "supreme commander" among the terms "president of the municipality," "president of the Assembly," were you talking about supreme commander in a technical sense, as in a job title, or you were just kind of talking about it metaphorically, as Judge Hoepfel is suggesting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have been one only, metaphorically speaking, because I already explained that he was not in command and it was evident that he was not commanding the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Black, the witness didn't use this word "supreme commander" among the terms "president of the municipality," "president of the Assembly," and so on, but before he mentioned these terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. It was subsequent sentences. That's why I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So it is possible that first it was more like a general idea than he went into specific offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I will move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Dragisic, Milan Martic led the Council for National Resistance, didn't he? He was given the position of staff commander by Milan Babic and then he led the council.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, definitely not, because Milan Babic did not entrust anyone with the task. He would not entrust anyone with any task that he would not assume upon himself. And not even by his position could he be that, because, as I said before, the National Resistance Council was made from the committee for All People's Defence and Socialist Protection. And the president of that committee was the president of the Assembly, and that particular office was held by Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I'm a bit confused, because, on the one hand, you tell me you don't know anything about the work of the Council for National Resistance, but you can tell me definitely that Milan Babic was in charge and not Milan Martic. How is that? Do you know about the work of the council or do you not know about the work of the council?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the work of the council, but I know how it functioned. The president of the Assembly; simultaneously the president of the council. You cannot have a policeman a president -- the president of the council or commander or what have you. It is the president of the Assembly who is at the same time the president of the council. And that was regulated thus under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So you're talking about how it should have been formally. But you don't know, in reality, how the council worked; is that what you're saying to me?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think it's a convenient time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, during the last session, you told us that Milan Martic was not in charge of the barricades. I would like you to look with me at a document. It's Exhibit 496 in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm interested in page 6, I think, both in B/C/S and in English. In English it has the ERN 02195509 at the top, and it is page 6 on the B/C/S translation. On my monitor I see the English version, whereas the witness will need to see the B/C/S version. Perfect. Thank you. If we could actually.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom it in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Let's zoom in on the bottom half. Oops, we just lost the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Is it one page you're showing?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. Just one paragraph, in fact, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: They're trying to get the B/C/S version on for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I have the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I have the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: While we're jumping from one to the other, may I ask you if the English or the B/C/S version is the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's the English version, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This is a transcript we received from the British Broadcasting Corp., the BBC in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Now we have the B/C/S on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, this is the transcript of an interview with Milan Martic on the 14th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if we could zoom in on the bottom half of this page in B/C/S, please. That's fine. Scroll down ever so slightly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it at all possible for us to get the English version? I've tried. Thanks. Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The English just came up on my screen, Your Honour. Do you have it now as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have it now, thanks to Judge Hoepfel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, focus with me on the first paragraph you see on your screen and just read along with me. It says: "On the 17th of August, two days before our referendum, we got an info that Croatia with its police had started to disarm the police stations in Serbian opstinas. In Knin, we allowed them to disarm us. In agreement with Raskovic and Babic, we decided to take all the weapons from the storages of the reserve militia and we made a false attempt as if the citizens broke into the storage. We took the arms, and from that moment I personally assumed command over the roadblocks. That was the first time we raised the barricades, but they were not meant to attack anyone, but to defend ourselves." Now, having seen that, these words of Milan Martic, do you now accept that Mr. Martic was in charge of the barricades?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of that council, and whether Milan Babic and Milan Martic agreed on anything and what that was, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So, do you accept Milan Martic was in charge of the barricades, or do you disagree? Or is it simply the case that you do not know one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was or was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You do know that he was a member of the Council for National Resistance, though; right? You said earlier that you don't accept that he was the leader of that council, but you do accept that he was a member; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of that council, and I cannot decidedly claim that he was. But by virtue of his office, heading the council had to be Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I guess the same kind of question as last time: Do you accept that Milan Martic was a member of the Council for National Resistance, do you deny it, or is it the case that you simply don't know whether or not he was a member?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know whether he was or was not a member, because, as I say, the council met and issued communiques. I myself was not a member of the council and I cannot assert who members of the council were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. It's true, isn't it, that the council existed outside of the ordinary political structures in Knin. For example, some of the members of the council didn't hold any political office at all. That's correct, isn't it? If you know. If you don't know, you can say that you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I replied a while ago that I wasn't a member and I don't know who the members of the council were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: At the time, in fact, you were the commander of the Knin TO. That was your position at this time; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you said how you were meeting with JNA officials. And my question is: Mustn't you have known what was going on with the barricades, who was organising them, who was coordinating them, what the status was, by virtue of your position as TO commander?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that they were being organised by the SDS and that they were being put up and that the activists and members of the SDS were manning the barricades -- manned the barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So you say you knew that, but you didn't know or don't know today that the Council for National Resistance was coordinating and organising the barricades. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You know, you've told us several times about positions of Milan Babic, and it seems like you know quite a bit about Milan Babic although very little about Milan Martic. And my question to you is: What you're really doing is trying to minimise anything that would implicate your brother-in-law by saying that Milan Babic was actually in control of everything. That's what's happening here today; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was the realistic situation where there was not a single duty that he could have assumed that he didn't actually take upon himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, in --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he was the man in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Milan Babic was a popular politician at the time and he held political power in Knin. But as to operational matters, that was the province of Milan Martic, right, from August 1990 onward?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He held all power in Knin, the political one, the operational one, and the real power was in his hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm correct, aren't I, that Milan Martic was named Secretary of the Interior in January of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the reason he was named to that position was because of his role in the summer and fall of 1990; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, but Babic appointed him and he was -- he had been an associate of Babic's from earlier times, and it was quite logical that he should be appointed to the post of secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: An associate of Babic's, you say, from earlier times, but you mean the summer and fall of 1990; right? That's when Milan Martic and Milan Babic were working together.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I just want to explore a couple of more topics with you about the Council for National Resistance. You said that you weren't familiar with its work, so if I ask you about something that you don't know about, you can just tell me that. But let me just see what you do know. Do you know that at some time in September, Milan Babic and a few other members of the council distanced themselves from the work of the Council for National Resistance?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you know that on the 10th of September, 1990, Milan Babic signed an agreement with Croatian authorities, including Minister of the Interior Bojkovac, to peacefully resolve the situation, including the returning the weapons that had been taken from the police stations? Did you know about that on the 10th of September?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact date, but I do know that Milan Babic had negotiated with Bojkovac and Vukas and other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And that agreement that Babic reached with those people, that was rejected by the Council for National Resistance. Milan Babic was even branded a traitor for negotiating that agreement; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: A couple of questions about the activities of the council. You have told us that the Council for National Resistance issued public communiques; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And those communiques commented on -- for instance, maybe they condemned the actions of Croatian authorities. They also gave instructions to the citizens about how to prepare for defence, those types of issues. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you are right. It was a long time ago. I don't remember exactly, but that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm correct, aren't I, that one of the main goals of this council was to create a situation or the circumstances which would bring about intervention of the JNA, a military intervention in Knin and the Krajina. That was one of their goals; right? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. What I do know is that the JNA sought to prevent any kind of conflict and to act in conformity with the law. The JNA also strove to prevent any types of conflicts and barricades, but the conflicts mounted anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you there. As part of its goal to bring about a military intervention, did you know that the council actually organised incidents such as blocking of rail traffic, blowing up of kiosks, and damage to private shops owned by Croats, in an attempt to justify a military intervention?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Between August and, let's say, December of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that any such actions were carried out in the area of Knin municipality in that period. Such actions only occurred in May 1991 and later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And, as far as you know, did the Council for National Resistance have anything to do with those incidents in May 1991 and later?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that the council had anything to do with it, but I know that Serbian weekend cottages were already being blown up in Zadar, Sibenik, and Split, and that Serbian shops in Croatian towns were being demolished, so that I believe that that was a reaction to such incidents. I do not think that it was coming from the national council.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You said in your testimony that Milan Babic became the head of government and Minister of Defence, I think you said, on the 29th of May, 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In fact, Milan Martic was elected Minister of Defence on that day, on the 29th of May, 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was elected Minister of the Interior, the police minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In fact, what happened - and correct me if I'm wrong about this - but Milan Martic was elected Minister of Defence but he did not assume that position. He remained, essentially, Minister of the Interior. He had been Secretary of the Interior before. And that's why the responsibilities of the Ministry of Defence fell on Milan Babic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Babic, as the prime minister designate, had the right to appoint ministers, and he kept the portfolio of Minister of Defence for himself. And Martic was reappointed from secretary to the Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It is actually one I hadn't intended to use. I apologise. It wasn't on my list. It is Exhibit 35 in evidence. Can we please see that on the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, if you see this document on the screen in front of you now, this document, which is dated -- well, it says: "On the 29th of May, 1991, Milan Martic was elected Minister of Defence," correct, "for the SAO Krajina"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this document, but I know for a fact that Martic never, never was the Minister of Defence, and that this was not actually put into practice. But Martic was the Minister of the Interior. This never went into effect. I can claim that. It was not implemented in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So I think we're in agreement on this. You're saying despite this document showing that he was elected Minister of Defence, in fact he maintained his portfolio of Secretary of the Interior and then later Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: We're done with that document. We can take it off the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, turning now to the subject of -- more specifically, the subject of the TO. From early 1991, I think you explained that -- and actually from around March of 1991, the Knin TO stopped having much contact with the Croatian TO. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And around that time, it was really more affiliated with the SAO Krajina authorities rather than the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time it was primarily affiliated with the 9th Corps command, up until the installing -- the establishment of this government on the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Just so it's clear, even -- well, at this time, the TO continued to be subordinated to the JNA if there were any need for combat operations, correct, the same as it had been before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Am I correct that, up until around the summer of 1991, there only existed municipal TOs in the Krajina. There was no larger TO body.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I think you explained how the TO in Krajina wasn't particularly well-developed in large part because most of the best men and weapons and equipment went to the JNA or the police. Am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to the police. And I said what the exact date was. It was the 24th or the 25th of June, where the partial mobilisation of the JNA was conducted. And I was asked then to have the able-bodied and militarily-capable people, to have them transferred to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the number.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Motorised Brigade of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can you repeat the number of the motorised brigade of the JNA. It wasn't understood by the translator.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 221st.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, it's nevertheless correct that at the time a lot of able young men were joining the police ranks as well as the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is possible. But as regards to the Territorial Defence members, I know that they were all transferred to the 221st Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You say "all" referring to, I take it, the Knin TO. That's what you're just talking about there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. I have no information about the other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And in this situation, the difficulty in recruiting men and the other difficulties faced by the TO, that was fairly widely known, at least among the JNA. Mr. Martic and other people knew about that situation; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably they did. Because at this meeting when the units were being transferred, that meeting was also attended by Milan Babic and the Secretary for National Defence in charge of mobilisation affairs, Sava Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony, it was said that you were appointed Acting Chief of Staff of the SAO Krajina TO in the summer of 1991. Could you give us the actual date, or at least a better approximation of when you were appointed acting Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There never was a written order. This was an oral order issued by the then president, i.e., Minister Milan Babic. So there never was an order in writing to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you retain command over the Knin TO once you assumed this position of Acting Chief of Staff of the SAO Krajina TO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because as chief of the TO staff of Krajina, there actually was no command to speak of. That was more of a formal duty, because Babic was preparing to establish the staff of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And actually, I'm not sure whether you answered me about the date or the approximate date in which you were appointed Acting Chief of Staff. Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was sometime in mid August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And, in fact, it was on the 1st of August, 1991, that the SAO Krajina TO was formally established as one component of the SAO Krajina armed forces, correct, the other component being the police?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know that the police was a component of the armed forces of the Krajina in my time, that is to say up until September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me look quickly at a document. It is Exhibit 31 in evidence. Sir, first, before we scroll down, you can see that that makes reference to an Assembly session held on the 1st of August, 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If you scroll down to Article 5, you will see it says there: "It is established that Territorial Defence and Special Purpose Units of Krajina Ministry of the Interior will make up the armed forces of the Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But not the police. Just units for special purposes. So within the ranks of the police, which numbered, let's say, 100, there were 50 men -- sorry, 10 men who formed a unit for special purposes. So it was not the entire police force, just one part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. That was my mistake on terminology. I was -- but these special units, they also pertained to the Ministry of the Interior; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the same way before and at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And even after this decision of the 1st of August, 1991, the SAO Krajina TO units and also the MUP special purpose units, they were subordinated to JNA units and commanders for combat operation purposes; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was envisaged that way in the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. In practice, did it happen that way? Or did it also happen in a different way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In fact, sometimes, at least, for the special purpose units, they were actually under a separate command but they coordinated with the JNA; is that correct? If you know. If you don't know about it, you can also say so.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That's correct. That's the way it was supposed to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: On the 2nd of August, 1991, Milan Babic, as Prime Minister, proclaimed himself the Supreme Commander of the SAO Krajina TO; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That was an attempt at, what you've described in your testimony, Milan Babic trying to take control of the TO and create a Serb army that he would be in command of; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I believe you testified that you opposed that, or you -- you preferred to coordinate with the JNA, and you opposed Babic's attempt to establish a separate Serb army; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I think you said also, just so that I'm clear, Milan Martic also opposed Babic's attempt to create a Serb army under Babic's control; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Milan Martic, like you, advocated cooperation with the JNA. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Am I also right that Milan Babic's attempts during 1991 to establish a Serb army under his control or to establish an effective SAO Krajina TO specifically under his control, was ultimately -- that was unsuccessful, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August and until the time the 12th of September, no. However, in the meantime, Milan Babic appointed General Djuic a retired JNA general, to be the commander of the TO Krajina. But at that time I had already been wounded and I was away for treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. I'm curious about that. What was the date that you received your injuries and you had to go to be treated in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 12th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In fact, notwithstanding the appointment of Mr. Djuic, Milan Martic remained de facto the commander of both the police and -- the special purpose units and the TO throughout 1991, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Police units, yes, but Milan Martic was certainly not commander of the TO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you deny that Milan Martic had any command position over the TO units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 12th of September, he had no command over TO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me show you Exhibit 37 on the screen, please. Mr. Dragisic, you will see that this is -- this is an order appointing Milan Martic the Deputy Commander of the Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina on the 8th of August, 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's an order issued by Babic, but that was never enforced on the ground. I'm talking about the period when I was there. At that time Milan Martic was not, definitely not, commander of the Territorial Defence, nor did he issue them any orders or anything. You will not find a single order signed by Milan Martic, because I never received any such order, not even this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let's have a look at some documents on this subject. In fact, even before the 8th of August, Milan Martic received reports and he issued orders to the Territorial Defence, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall receiving any orders signed by Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can we please see Exhibit 39 on the e-court. You will see that this is -- actually, if we could scroll up to the top again, of the document, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, you will see that this is a report from the SAO Krajina staff dated the 19th of July, 1991. And I'm correct, aren't I, that one of the addressees is the secretary of the SUP for SAO Krajina, which is Milan Martic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you can also see that this is a report dealing with the situation on the ground from the TO staff. You're a man with military experience. Reports such as this one ordinarily only go to people who are involved in decision-making; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you scroll it up?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. If you can scroll down there. Perfect. Maybe all the way. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: My question was: A report like this ordinarily is only addressed to those people who may be involved in the decision-making on the issues in the report; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were also sent for information to people who needed to know. Milan Martic probably received this because he had under his control special police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let's look at another document. It is Exhibit 38 in evidence. And if we could -- that's perfect right there. Before we go on to the content, Mr. Dragisic, you see that this is a report from the SAO Krajina TO staff dated the 6th of August, 1991. And if you look at the first paragraph of the order -- excuse me, of the report, it says: "Milan Martic has issued an order for a cease-fire, except in the event of a direct attack." So that refers to an order issued by Milan Martic, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the reason why Milan Martic could issue such an order, a general cease-fire order, was because de facto he was the person in charge of not just the police but also the TO, which is the body from which this document originates; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, I have no comment on this. But I know that he was not my commander, nor did he issue any orders to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But he could issue an order for a cease-fire which you were obligated to respect; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me look at another document. This one is 65 ter number 2052, if we could see that on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just get clarity. You just said that: "I'm telling you, I have no comment on this. But I know that he was not my commander, nor did he issue any orders to me." Now you have accepted that he could issue an order for a cease-fire which you were obligated to respect. He was your commander, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot accept that he was the commander, because the truth is the Supreme Commander was Milan Babic. As for Martic, in that period --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because, you see, this refers to an area outside of Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- this document is addressed to the supreme commander, amongst other people. Yes, we understand who the supreme commander is. All I'm saying is, he was your commander because you were obligated to respect an order he issued. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And now if we could see 65 ter number 2052, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, e-court froze. I am just reloading it right now. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Oh, yes, there we see it. There we have the B/C/S up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, this document now, this is another report by the SAO Krajina TO staff and it's dated the 2nd of September, 1991. I see that it's -- there are several addressees, the Supreme Commander of the SAO Krajina TO, the Commander of the SAO Krajina TO, the Chief of the SAO Krajina TO, and then the State Security Section. Are you one of those addressees? Do one of these titles apply to you at the time, on the 2nd of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief of TO of SAOK, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we can -- it's just at the very bottom of your screen right now. You will see a paragraph that says: "After the Secretary Milan Martic requested the reports from the field, the reports arrived in the following order." And then you see reference to reports from Kistanje, Plasko, Donji Lapac, Benkovac, and some other places. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it says that Milan Martic is the secretary, not commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right, right. And it says that he requested reports from the field, and then the reports arrived in the following order; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could we exhibit this, admit this document into evidence, Your Honour, please, and give it an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 957.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could now see Exhibit 40 in evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dragisic, this is another report from the SAO Krajina TO staff, although it is dated the 17th of September, 1991, which is after you said you were out of the area. I just want you to be aware of that date. But I am going to ask you to look at part of the document. You can see, just a couple of paragraphs down, it says: "At 1750 hours, Secretary Milan Martic issued the following order," and then it shows four numbered things there; the first one says: "For the Benkovac staff." The fourth one, "For the Kistanje staff." This document shows Milan Martic giving orders to TO staffs, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, Milan Martic was the Secretary of the Interior, that is Minister of the Interior, and he had police affairs in his jurisdiction. Now, from this report, we see that JNA units were under blockade in their barracks, and an attempt to lift that blockade was made. So Milan Martic's orders referred to police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But it says quite clearly right here, doesn't it, "issued order for the Benkovac staff." This is a SAO Krajina TO document. That's a reference to the Benkovac TO staff, not to the police; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which men are meant. But as far as TO Benkovac staff is concerned, the commander of that staff was Zoran, and I don't remember his last name. He was the commander of TO Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And this document refers to an order to him or, in any event, to the Benkovac staff. I mean, that has to be a reference to the TO staff, not to police; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the same, I guess, is true for when it refers to the Kistanje staff, at number 4 there. It's a little hard to see, but ...

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you see that Milan Martic is referred to as the secretary, and in the TO there were no secretaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. I think we're in agreement that at the time of this, in September of 1991, Milan Martic was the Secretary or the Minister of the Interior; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minister, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. But nevertheless, as I think we just agreed, this appears to refer to orders to TO staffs in Benkovac and Kistanje. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all for that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You were just thinking of the name of this commander of the TO Benkovac. So was it maybe ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zoran Lakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Not Tatic, Lakic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lakic, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, I'm going to shift topics slightly and turn your attention to the attack on Kijevo on the 26th of August, 1991. You made reference to operations in Kijevo, I believe, on that date. You said that the JNA conducted operations in Kijevo. In fact, the police, or at least the special purpose units of the Ministry of the Interior, also participated in that operation in Kijevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes. Because the operation was led by the commander of the 222nd brigade, Colonel Djukic, with his units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And police units also participated; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And they were resubordinated and Colonel Djukic commanded over them, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you participate in the operation in Kijevo at the end of August?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you hear about the destruction in the village; that the church was destroyed, that a lot of houses were burned, that other civilian buildings were damaged or destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the operation, the artillery was probably engaged as well as the air force. And if they were involved, there were probably buildings destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And you say "there were probably buildings destroyed." Did you hear about such destruction, or you didn't hear anything about it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I heard was that there were buildings destroyed, since the air force was engaged, but I wasn't in that area at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You also testified a little bit about blockades of JNA facilities. Those blockades began around September 1991, maybe the end of August; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually, going back a little bit in 1991. You testified a little bit about Plitvice and the clash there, and I think you mentioned that some Krajina policemen or special purpose members were taken prisoner by the Croatian police forces; is that right? Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: At that time, the SAO Krajina police was also taking Croatian policemen prisoner; is that right? At that same time of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not then but later. At the negotiations that Babic held with the president of the municipality of Sinj, Vukas, Mr. Vukas, Croatia did not release the policeman who had been captured. And from that time on, some Croatian policemen were taken prisoner, first and foremost, to be later exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what's the date that you say that that first started happening, that Croatian policemen were taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think around end of May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can we see Exhibit 204 on the e-court, please. And I apologise, this is another document that I did not intend to use and so it was not on my list. But we will just look at it briefly, given the witness's answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, I apologise, this is a document that is only in English, but I'm just going to refer to it as quickly as I can. It's a newspaper article from the 2nd of April, 1991, from the Yugoslav News Agency. Oops. Now, actually we have a translation, so you can probably read along better than I can, because my e-court has stopped working.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could have two minutes to be able to see the English on this, I just need to restart my e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Are you sure it's Exhibit 204? This is a BBC document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I believe it says the source is Tanjug, but, Your Honour, I can't read the English right now so I'm a little bit disabled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We can read the English to you. It says: "World Broadcast, 1991, the British Broadcasting Corporation/BBC, 4th of April," not 2nd, "4th of April, 1991, Thursday."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. And a little further down, if I can rely on the B/C/S version which I see on my screen, because it's a summary of a world broadcast, the actual source of this information is from Tanjug on the 2nd of April, if I am not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Do you want me to repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I have it in English now, Your Honour, thank you. I apologise for the delay here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for the delay, Mr. Dragisic. If you look at the first paragraph there, there's a reference to Milan Martic, Secretary of the SUP of Krajina, and it says: "According to him, the Krajina police have arrested six Croatian constables. Four were arrested on the 31st of March, near Plasko, and two on the 1st and 2nd of April, near Civljane." Having seen that statement attributed to Mr. Martic, do you accept the possibility that even earlier than May, 1991, the SAO Krajina police was taking some Croatian policemen prisoner?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I accept that they did arrest them, and I explained what the reason for that was; that in Plitvice, 13 or 16, I don't remember exactly, member of the special police units of the Krajina, the Krajina militia, were taken prisoner. And as they would not release them, we were looking for every possibility of how to obtain such a release. So they arrested Croatian policemen in order to exchange them for the former.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If you will look with me, just one details, it does say that six people were actually arrested on the 31st of March, which is the same day that Plitvice happened; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In any event, in Plitvice, what ended the armed clash there was that the JNA stepped in as a sort of buffer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the same thing happened at the beginning of May in the clash that you referred to in Borovo Selo. There was fighting between Serb and Croatian police and the JNA stepped in as a buffer; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that was in fact the legal obligation of the JNA, because that was at the time when the SFRY still existed and when those laws were still in force. Had it not acted in that way, it would have been in breach of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was Milan Martic president -- president, excuse me -- present in Borovo Selo on the 1st or 2nd of May, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that with certainty. I don't know what his movements were at the time. I don't think he was, but I cannot recall where he was. I know for a fact that I, myself, was not outside my own area. I cannot say where he was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. As we saw a little earlier, in August, 1991, the JNA participated along with the police in an attack on Kijevo at the end of August; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kijevo, Croatia had established a police station, and it prevented all citizens from the area of Cetina and Civan [phoen] from passing through. And they were under this blockade for over a month. It only let JNA APCs through.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry. We don't need to go into much more detail. Since you mentioned the police station, those were the only Croatian forces in Kijevo, right, the Croatian police station? There wasn't any other kind of armed force in Kijevo, in August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't. But around there, there were at least 300 armed men, including some Albanians who had come to join in the war. There were not only police units there. There were also paramilitary forces of the Croatian Zengas, the National Guards Corps of Croatia. Because, under the law at the time, the only forces were the JNA and the TO, whereas the National Peoples Guard Corps was there, which was, in effect, a paramilitary unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So when you refer to 300 armed men, you're referring to the Zengas, the ZNG; right? Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you say they were actually in Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the numbers included Albanians, at least some Albanians, you say.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just a few minutes ago you referred to the duty of the JNA to act as a buffer. But it's clear by the events of Kijevo that, in fact, the JNA at that time was abandoning any sort of neutral role and it was actively taking the side of the Krajina Serbs in their conflict with Croatia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA, i.e., the 9th Corps, i.e., the 221st Brigade had their zone of responsibility which included Kijevo. But they were not able to pass through Kijevo. So there was no police station before the war in Kijevo. This one that was there then was actually established illegally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to get into the legality of the Croatian MUP establishing a police station in its own territory. But it's clear in Kijevo that the SAO Krajina forces and the JNA forces acted in coordination and cooperation with one another; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Which takes me back to the issue of the blockades. Is it fair to say that by blockading JNA facilities in -- starting in around September 1991, Croatia was really trying to reestablish control over the TO weapons that had been seized and neutralize the JNA in Croatia, because it was seeing the JNA as taking the Serb side in the emerging conflict? Is that a fair, I guess, explanation of what Croatia thought it was doing in blockading the JNA facilities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian side, and I repeat, blockaded illegally - illegally - the only legitimate armed force in their barracks, and the instructions to each combat unit were that, in case they were attacked, they should respond, strike back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The instructions to which combat units? I'm just not 100 per cent clear. Croatian combat units or the JNA combat units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA units had instructions. Every unit of the JNA, according to the laws on All National Defence of the SFRY and of the Republic of Croatia which were then in force, had that obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. We just have a few minutes left but let me try to get through one more topic with you, Mr. Dragisic. You were an instructor at the School for Internal Affairs in Golubic beginning in June of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were there any other police training facilities at Golubic besides the one that you taught at?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you testified that those who completed training there, they were eligible to be patrolmen but they didn't participate in any combat operations; correct? That's what you testified to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: First of all, you would agree with me that the training at Golubic in 1991 did include combat aspects; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that has nothing to do with the training which was delivered in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The training in 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but you agree that in 1991 it was combat-oriented.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And even in 1992, there were some combat elements of the training that went on at Golubic, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We only had shooting from infantry weapons. Otherwise the training was, as for peacetime training, according to the plan of training for patrolmen. There was no other training apart from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If I could have just a moment of your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, I appreciate your patience with my questions. I don't have any further questions for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you, and I imagine it's time to end for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: For Mr. Black that ends our session, or invites the ending. We had left an issue for the end of the day, and I wonder if we could just quickly address it, which was the date to be set for the Defence motion to be filed with respect to the statements. I think that Defence indicated that they could address that at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we had brief consultations and the situation is as follows: It will be possible for some of the first witnesses, after this short break that we will be having, will be witnesses according to 87(F) or 92 bis. We have to process them first as witnesses, that is our first task, and we are working very actively on it. It is quite difficult for us to tell you exactly within what time we can do that. These statements have to be translated into English; submitted to the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber. We shall do that as fast as -- as quickly and efficiently as we can, bearing in mind also the need for the Prosecution team to prepare themselves and that they need more than a day or two prior to the testimony of the witness. But I cannot tell you exactly we can fulfil our obligation for all witnesses on that particular day, because they are quite a few. Now, depending on what witnesses come, perhaps the sequence might be changed and the urgencies may be reversed. That is also what I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I understood Mr. Whiting earlier today, he indicated that they would need at least a week, not a day or two. But that's something that you can sort out between the two of you. Can you give us a date, at least, by when the witnesses that you are going to be calling in the first week when we come back can be given?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you will allow me to give you that piece of information tomorrow. I will have the list after this break and we will have definite information tomorrow. It is also associated, as far as we are concerned, with travel documents which have to be issued for the witnesses and some safety considerations. But, by your leave, I can give you precise information in the morning, rather than give you unverified verified facts right now. At any rate, we shall certainly do our best for the Prosecution to have these statements with at least a week's notice prior to the actual appearance of the witness in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, just two points. First, we've already been told what witnesses are going to be appearing after the break, at least three of them. So if there is some change to that, we certainly would appreciate knowing that as soon as possible. The second thing is: The point I was trying to make is not simply that we need them a week ahead of time. That we do. But I think a motion needs to be filed even in the advance of that so that it can be determined whether these can be -- come in and how and under what Rule. So it cannot be that we receive these one week ahead of time. This has to be done long before that. And if it's done in batches, that, I completely understand. Maybe it cannot be done for all 23 at once, but certainly it can be done for a chunk with sufficient time for the -- for us to respond, the Court to consider it, and a decision to be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Milovancevic? The motion is to come in before, and then you still have to do that afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do hear you. Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. We shall do so as promptly as possible. Tomorrow morning we will be able to tell you when we can do that, the actual statements for the first witnesses, when those can be had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that okay? Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. While we are at it, Mr. Milovancevic, there is something that has been going on in my mind. Sometime last week there were two statements that you tendered which were in B/C/S and we thought they needed to be translated. We then found out that the one was translated and then the other we took to have been translated. I don't know if you still remember. Having such a poor memory like I do, I'm not able to tell you what document that was. But I just know that there is a document that needs to be -- it's about a page or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two documents, Your Honour. The title pages of the book that I showed. Thank you for the reminder. I don't know the exact mark of the page right now, because I mislaid it. But thank you, Your Honour. I shall certainly bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court is adjourned for the day. We will reconvene tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. Court adjourned.
